title: Salesforce System Architect Primer: Course Completion Exam
description: Timed practice exam covering the whole series. Pass with 72% or higher to earn the course completion certificate.

questions.question: An architect needs a single REST call that creates an Account, a Contact tied to its new ID, and a Case, all together. Which tool and which limit does the lesson direct them to?
options: The Composite resource, which runs up to 25 subrequests in one call with subrequests able to reference each other's results by ID.
A plain external web service call, because Composite only works when every subrequest talks to an external system.
Separate REST calls, because Composite requests cannot reference each other's results.
Composite Graph, because a plain Composite request is capped at five subrequests.
questions.explanation: The lesson defines Composite as letting a single API request carry up to 25 subrequests that Salesforce runs and returns as one response, with subrequests able to reference each other's results by ID. Composite Graph raises the ceiling to 500 for deep dependency trees, and plain Composite allows more than five subrequests.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Security, Part 2: Profiles, Permission Sets, Permission Set Groups, MFA, and Session Policies”, what is the central focus?
options: Who can do what in an org. The move from profile-led to permission-set-led access, what a permission set group bundles together, the 2026 MFA enforcement that now touches every login, and the session policies that decide how long a session lives.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: Who can do what in an org. The move from profile-led to permission-set-led access, what a permission set group bundles together, the 2026 MFA enforcement that now touches every login, and the session policies that decide how long a session lives.

questions.question: An architect changes an Account record's default currency from EUR to USD. Based on the lesson, what happens to the existing currency amounts on that record?
options: They are immediately revalued at the current exchange rate.
They are not converted; they display with the new currency code.
They are converted through the corporate currency in two steps.
The change is blocked unless Advanced Currency Management is enabled.
questions.explanation: Changing the default currency of a record does not convert its amounts; they simply display with the new currency code. The two-step record-to-corporate-to-personal conversion applies when a value is actually converted, not when the record's currency label is changed.

questions.question: A field-services company wants a technician assistant that answers from its product manuals and can also open follow-up service cases. It currently routes all model traffic through the API gateway that already fronts its REST services. Which gap in that choice does the lesson identify?
options: The gateway rate-limits by request and caches by exact match, so a user can exhaust the budget in long documents and repeated questions reaccrue cost with no multi-provider failover.
The gateway handles token-based rate limiting but not semantic caching, so it should be replaced to save money.
The gateway is fine for model traffic as long as it uses a single provider, because LLM calls behave like any other API call.
The gateway should be removed entirely so each application can pick its own model and provider directly.
questions.explanation: The lesson's first pitfall is that a plain API gateway measures the wrong thing: it rate-limits by request when LLM cost and capacity scale with tokens, caches by exact match so repeated questions reaccrue cost, and fronts a single provider with no failover, which is why the fix is an LLM gateway that understands tokens.

questions.question: A nightly integration must upsert 250,000 product records into Salesforce. A developer proposes one REST call per record. Using the lesson's reasoning, what is the correct design and why?
options: Keep the per-record REST design, because the daily request allocation is large enough to absorb 250,000 calls.
Move the load to Bulk API 2.0, because any operation over roughly 2,000 records belongs there and its ingest batches draw from the separate 15,000-batch pool rather than the daily request allocation.
Keep the per-record design but schedule it during business hours so it is metered against interactive user traffic.
Move the load to Platform Events, because event publishes do not count toward any allocation.
questions.explanation: The lesson states that any operation over about 2,000 records belongs in Bulk API 2.0, and that Bulk API has its own separate allocation of 15,000 batches per rolling 24 hours shared with Bulk API, with ingest jobs consuming batches. The cost unit is the call, not the record, so per-record REST turns a modest bulk job into hundreds of thousands of calls.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: The opposite is true: lesson 26 taught you how to design the REST integration itself.
The lesson claims this cannot be verified at all.
Lesson 26 taught you how to design the REST integration itself.
The lesson recommends treating output as final without review.
questions.explanation: Lesson 26 taught you how to design the REST integration itself.

options: The observability layer of a Salesforce org: debug logs and trace flags when a transaction misbehaves, Event Monitoring when you need who, what, and when across the whole org, health checks for the security baseline and the platform status, and the alerting that turns all of it into action instead of archaeology.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The observability layer of a Salesforce org: debug logs and trace flags when a transaction misbehaves, Event Monitoring when you need who, what, and when across the whole org, health checks for the security baseline and the platform status, and the alerting that turns all of it into action instead of archaeology.

questions.question: A customer files a GDPR subject access request asking what personal data the org holds on them. Per the lesson, what must the org be able to do, and what makes it possible?
options: Assemble every record that touches the person across objects, which a single customer identifier and a clean data model make possible, because personal data is spread across accounts, cases, and transactions.
Delete the customer's records immediately, because the right of access is satisfied by erasure.
Export the Setup Audit Trail, because configuration changes are the only personal data the GDPR covers.
Move the customer's data to a non-EU region, because residency overrides the right of access.
questions.explanation: The right of access means the org must assemble every record touching the person across objects. A single customer identifier and a clean data model make that assembly possible, since personal data is spread across accounts, cases, and transactions.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Solution Design: Turning a Requirement Into an Architecture Document (NFRs and Tradeoffs)”, what is the central focus?
options: How a requirement becomes an architecture document: separating the business why from the what and the how, writing measurable non-functional requirements using the Salesforce Well-Architected framework (Trusted, Easy, Adaptable), resolving design tradeoffs explicitly, and recording each decision with its rationale so the delivery team can build without re-litigating every choice.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: How a requirement becomes an architecture document: separating the business why from the what and the how, writing measurable non-functional requirements using the Salesforce Well-Architected framework (Trusted, Easy, Adaptable), resolving design tradeoffs explicitly, and recording each decision with its rationale so the delivery team can build without re-litigating every choice.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: The lesson says the opposite: this should always be avoided.
"Architect" is not the most overloaded title in the Salesforce ecosystem.
"Architect" is the most overloaded title in the Salesforce ecosystem.
The lesson recommends treating output as final without review.
questions.explanation: "Architect" is the most overloaded title in the Salesforce ecosystem.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Security, Part 3: External Access, OAuth, SAML/SSO, Connected Apps, and Communities”, what is the central focus?
options: How outside systems and outside people get in. OAuth flows for machine access, SAML single sign-on for employee logins, connected apps as the doorway, and Experience Cloud communities as the portal where customers and partners authenticate without touching your internal identity system.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: How outside systems and outside people get in. OAuth flows for machine access, SAML single sign-on for employee logins, connected apps as the doorway, and Experience Cloud communities as the portal where customers and partners authenticate without touching your internal identity system.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what is the single load-bearing difference between a workflow and an agent?
options: A workflow is fixed code paths orchestrating LLMs and tools, while an agent lets the LLM dynamically direct its own process and tool usage.
A workflow uses many models while an agent uses one model.
A workflow never calls tools while an agent always does.
A workflow runs on a server while an agent runs on a client device.
questions.explanation: Anthropic's distinction is that a workflow orchestrates LLMs and tools through predefined code paths, while an agent lets the LLM dynamically direct its own process and tool usage, maintaining control over how it accomplishes the task.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Flow is the right tool for a process that must roll back cleanly or commit partially on a boundary condition.
Transactional control makes a process an Apex problem, because Flow has no access to Database.savepoint or Database.rollback.
Flow and Apex express transactional control equally well, so the choice comes down to developer preference.
When a process coordinates an ERP, a WMS, and finance, the orchestration belongs in a trigger so the handoff stays inside Salesforce.
questions.explanation: A savepoint and rollback requirement is an Apex requirement, not a Flow shortcoming to work around, and cross-system orchestration belongs in the external layer that owns those systems.

questions.question: Which statement about the cutover violates the lesson's guidance?
options: The dry run at production volume surfaces lock contention, DML-limit failures, and validation rejections that a small test load hides.
Writes to both source orgs are frozen for the entire cutover window before the final snapshot is extracted.
Automation is suppressed during the bulk load by a controlled, business-approved bypass, then re-enabled before the org opens.
The load runs over an S2S shared-record connection because it is the fastest native path and does not need a mapping or external IDs.
questions.explanation: S2S retires in Spring '27 and a durable consolidation deliberately exports and reloads through bulk tools with external-ID keys; a plan that leans on S2S to share the object set is short-lived and does not fit the lesson's guidance.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Testing Integrations: Mocking, Sandbox Test Strategy, and Integration Test Suites”, a ClaimSubmissionService calls an external clearinghouse. Why can a test not simply call the real endpoint, and what does a mock actually establish?
options: Because callouts in a test are slow but still reach the real service, so mocks only exist to speed the suite up.
Because real callouts are not made in test context, so you implement HttpCalloutMock, register it with Test.setMock, and write one test per response shape so the mock encodes the contract.
Because a mock is a way to make a failing test pass when the vendor API happens to be unavailable.
Because callout logic cannot be covered by tests at all and has to be verified manually before release.
questions.explanation: The platform refuses the network call during a test, so a mock is the specification of the seam: a success shape, an error shape, and a malformed payload each pin down how your code should behave.

questions.question: In the enterprise AI reference architecture, where does each of the three patterns sit in the stack?
options: RAG spans the data layer and AI/ML layer via a vector store plus retrieval and generation; the agent platform is the agentic layer runtime; the LLM gateway is the model entry point in the AI/ML layer.
RAG sits entirely in the data layer, the agent platform in the infrastructure layer, and the LLM gateway in the experience layer.
All three are components of the integration layer and interchangeable with the API gateway.
The agent platform does RAG and the LLM gateway, so the three are the same component with different names.
questions.explanation: The lesson places RAG where the data layer meets the AI/ML layer (a vector database stores embeddings while retrieval and generation live in the AI/ML layer), the agent platform in the agentic layer as the runtime for reasoning, memory, and tools, and the LLM gateway as the single model entry point in the AI/ML layer.

questions.question: An architect discovers that an accepted ADR's decision no longer applies because the ERP vendor changed its API rate limits. According to the lesson, what is the correct way to handle the record?
options: Edit the accepted ADR in place so it reflects the new vendor terms and current practice.
Delete the record and replace it with an updated design document section.
Write a new ADR that supersedes it, change the old record's status to Superseded, and point to the replacement.
Change the old record's status back to Proposed so the team can debate it again.
questions.explanation: The lesson states that an accepted ADR is immutable. When circumstances change, the team writes a new record that supersedes the old one, and the old record stays in place with its status changed to Superseded and a pointer to its replacement. Editing it in place destroys the historical integrity of the log, and deleting it removes the record of what the team believed at the time.

questions.question: Two orgs each hold a record for the same company as “Acme Corp” and “ACME Corporation”, and each record owns opportunities. Per the lesson, where does the decision to collapse them into one master record belong, and how do the losing record's children survive?
options: In production during cutover, where the winner is chosen by whichever record loads last, and orphans are cleaned up afterward.
In the mapping workbook before any load, where a dedup rule picks the master and the losing record's children reparent onto the winner through the external ID.
In the configuration track, where merging the picklists automatically dedups both records and their children.
Nowhere, because Salesforce will not permit two accounts inside the single consolidated org.
questions.explanation: Dedup is a mapping-workbook decision made before loading; the children reparent onto the chosen master through the external ID rather than being left orphaned.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance on tool permissions?
options: A read-only tool on sensitive data is harmless, because reading cannot change state.
Tool scoping is a one-time decision made at deployment, and later agent actions do not change it.
Every tool is both a capability and an attack surface, so the tool set should stay minimal and each tool's parameter space should be bounded, with human approval on high-impact actions.
The security of an agent is determined by the model's refusal policy, not by the tools it holds.
questions.explanation: The lesson argues the model is not the dangerous part; the tools are. A read tool is still half of an exfiltration, tool scope has to be sized per task and rechecked as actions change, and high-impact actions belong behind a human gate.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The daily total is the sum of a base amount, a per-license contribution, and any purchased add-ons.
The lesson argues this applies only in unrelated settings.
The lesson recommends treating output as final without review.
The daily total is not the sum of a base amount, a per-license contribution, and any purchased add-ons.
questions.explanation: The daily total is the sum of a base amount, a per-license contribution, and any purchased add-ons.

questions.question: An org has Advanced Currency Management enabled with dated exchange rates. Per the lesson, which of the following conversions does NOT use the dated exchange rate?
options: An opportunity that closed last quarter, valued at the rate in force that month.
An opportunity product line item amount.
A currency formula field result on the opportunity.
A currency amount in a report related to opportunities.
questions.explanation: Dated exchange rates are not used when calculating formula fields with a return type of Currency, nor in forecasting, currency fields on other objects, or other report types. They are used for opportunities, opportunity products, schedules, campaign opportunity fields, opportunity splits, and related reports.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Environment and Release Strategy: Sandbox Types, Change Sets vs DevOps (sf/sfdx)”, what is the central focus?
options: Where work happens and how it moves to production. The four sandbox types (Developer, Developer Pro, Partial Copy, Full), what each copies and how often it refreshes, then the release-mechanism fork: click-based change sets versus source-driven deployment with the sf CLI and a Git-based source of truth, including Salesforce DX and DevOps Center.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: Where work happens and how it moves to production. The four sandbox types (Developer, Developer Pro, Partial Copy, Full), what each copies and how often it refreshes, then the release-mechanism fork: click-based change sets versus source-driven deployment with the sf CLI and a Git-based source of truth, including Salesforce DX and DevOps Center.

questions.question: Per the lesson, an architect sets a solution SLO at 99.5% while the platform SLA is 99.9%. Why is staying below the platform number the right call?
options: Because a solution SLO must always be more stringent than the platform SLA to protect users.
Because matching the platform SLA leaves no error budget for application-layer failures, integration issues, or planned maintenance in the same measurement window.
Because the platform SLA is a hard cap that a solution SLO can never exceed.
Because 99.5% is the highest availability any Salesforce solution can realistically achieve.
questions.explanation: If the platform SLA and the solution SLO are both 99.9%, any significant platform downtime consumes the entire error budget, leaving no buffer for the failure classes the architect owns.

questions.question: An ERP requires XML while Salesforce uses JSON, and a review asks why the integration defines one internal canonical Customer contract instead of mapping each pair of systems directly. Which reasoning does the lesson give?
options: A canonical model converts N-times-M source-to-target mappings into N plus M, which is why it makes the translator family maintainable as more systems join.
A canonical model removes the need for any translators because every system adopts the same binary payload over the wire.
A canonical model only helps when there are exactly two systems, so it is the wrong choice for a many-system integration.
A canonical model is required by External Services and cannot be built in Apex.
questions.explanation: The lesson says translating every source to every target is N-times-M translations, while translating each source to one canonical model and each target from it is N plus M, and it calls the Canonical Data Model the translator family's organizing principle that keeps integrations maintainable as systems join.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Lightning Web Components Architecture: Composition, Wire Service, and Data Services”, a child component dispatches a CustomEvent that a grandparent utility panel must hear. What event configuration is required?
options: bubbles: true only, because composed is implied once a shadow root exists.
bubbles: true and composed: true, because the event has to bubble up and cross a shadow boundary.
composed: true only, because events bubble by default.
Neither, because Lightning web components use only the capture phase for dispatch and listening.
questions.explanation: bubbles defaults to false and composed defaults to false, so a direct parent needs bubbles and only an event that must cross a shadow root adds composed.

questions.question: Why does choosing a Lightning base component resolve most contrast and keyboard work in a Salesforce build?
options: Because base components disable custom styling entirely.
Because base components contain accessible SLDS markup, follow the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide, and meet or exceed WCAG 2.1 AA contrast.
Because base components automatically pass all WCAG AAA criteria.
Because base components replace the need for real form labels.
questions.explanation: Base components include accessible HTML markup from SLDS, follow the W3C ARIA Authoring Practices Guide for keyboard behavior and ARIA management, and conform to SLDS color guidelines that meet or exceed WCAG 2.1 AA contrast. That is why preferring base components is the highest-leverage accessibility decision.

questions.question: A business asks the integration team why a case changed status. Which statement best reflects what Change Data Capture can and cannot answer?
options: CDC records the state change but not the reason or intent behind it, so the team needs an explicit business event captured at the point of the action for the why.
CDC always includes the user action and intent behind each change in its header fields.
CDC cannot capture deletes or undeletes, so it is incomplete for auditing.
CDC is the only way to record the business reason for a change and replaces the need for platform events.
questions.explanation: CDC captures row-level state changes in committed order; it does not carry the intent, user, or reason behind the change. For the why, an explicit business event is required.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Denormalization should be avoided entirely, because every stored copy is duplicated state.
A roll-up summary is platform-maintained denormalization that keeps the cached value current, but it requires a master-detail relationship and adds write cost on every child change.
A cross-object formula field stores its value and can be indexed, which makes it the faster option at high volume.
A hand-written trigger that maintains a count field is preferable because you control exactly when it updates.
questions.explanation: A roll-up summary gives a read without an aggregate query and the platform keeps the copies straight, at the price of a master-detail commitment, write cost on the parent, and a finite per-object budget.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Isolation is enforced at the physical layer too: all platform data, metadata, and pivot tables are partitioned by OrgID using native database partitioning.
Isolation is not enforced at the physical layer too: all platform data, metadata, and pivot tables are partitioned by OrgID using native database partitioning.
The lesson states this is never a relevant consideration.
The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
questions.explanation: Isolation is enforced at the physical layer too: all platform data, metadata, and pivot tables are partitioned by OrgID using native database partitioning.

questions.question: Emergency changes are 28 percent of a client's production changes, and the CAB responds by requiring more approvals on the emergency path. Why does the lesson call that the wrong fix?
options: Emergency volume is unrelated to process design and should be tracked only for audit purposes.
A high emergency share means the normal path is too slow or unpredictable, so tightening the emergency path leaves the cause in place and pushes teams to bypass governance another way.
Emergencies should be blocked entirely, because production defects never justify an unplanned change.
The right fix is to remove the emergency tier and route every change through the major tier for consistency.
questions.explanation: The lesson treats emergency inflation as a process defect: teams declare emergencies because waiting on the normal path costs more. The fix is to measure normal lead time, find the waiting, and shorten the normal path, not to add friction to the only route that currently works.

questions.question: During the design scenario, a candidate wants to keep the order view fresh by calling the ERP for order status every time a rep opens an account. Why does the lesson direct the candidate away from making this an unbounded synchronous fan-in?
options: Because the trivial case is fine but the sum of synchronous callouts in a single Apex transaction is capped at 100 with a 120-second cumulative timeout, so the strategy must decide which flows can be synchronous at all.
Because Salesforce does not support more than one outbound callout per transaction.
Because the ERP owns fulfillment and therefore cannot be called for status at all.
Because a canonical data model removes the need to read external data in real time.
questions.explanation: The lesson states the platform limit explicitly: a single Apex transaction can make at most 100 callouts and 120 seconds of cumulative callout time. That constraint means the strategy assigns each flow a synchronous or asynchronous seam deliberately, and it is what pushes the unreliable ERP off the request path.

questions.question: Meridian must protect a regulated field that it does not need to filter or sort on. Which encryption decision does the lesson direct the architect to make?
options: Use volume-level encryption only, because it is always on and uses a Salesforce-managed key, and no field-level scheme is needed.
Add Shield Platform Encryption with a deterministic scheme, because deterministic encryption is the most secure option.
Add Shield Platform Encryption with a probabilistic scheme, because probabilistic encryption is the most secure and Meridian does not need to filter or sort on the field.
Skip encryption at rest and rely on encryption in transit, because the data only moves between systems.
questions.explanation: The lesson says to encrypt probabilistically by default and reserve deterministic encryption for fields you must filter or sort on. Since Meridian does not need to filter or sort on the regulated field, probabilistic encryption is the right scheme, and it is the most secure because identical values do not encrypt to identical ciphertext.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: The lesson argues this applies only in unrelated settings.
It sits between the ERP, the e-commerce platform, the marketing automation tool, and a dozen SaaS apps, and every one of them never requires to move records in and out.
The lesson claims this cannot be verified at all.
It sits between the ERP, the e-commerce platform, the marketing automation tool, and a dozen SaaS apps, and every one of them needs to move records in and out.
questions.explanation: It sits between the ERP, the e-commerce platform, the marketing automation tool, and a dozen SaaS apps, and every one of them needs to move records in and out.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The opposite is true: the client sends a username and password to the token endpoint.
The lesson claims this cannot be verified at all.
The client sends a username and password to the token endpoint.
The lesson recommends treating output as final without review.
questions.explanation: The client sends a username and password to the token endpoint.

questions.question: Per the lesson, why does pre-launch testing alone fail as a governance control for an AI model, when it works for a normal application?
options: Because a model's output distribution shifts as the data feeding it changes or a vendor releases a new version, so a pre-launch review is necessary but not sufficient and ongoing monitoring is part of the governance structure.
Because model outputs are always correct in production regardless of how they were tested, so testing wastes effort that should go to deployment.
Because a model's behavior is deterministic after ship, so a single pre-launch sign-off permanently guarantees safety.
Because the EU AI Act forbids any testing of minimal-risk systems, leaving pre-launch checks pointless.
questions.explanation: A model is not stable after ship: its output distribution shifts as the data or the vendor version changes, so governance requires continuous monitoring as part of the structure, not just a one-time pre-launch check.

questions.question: A release deploys successfully but a flow the release touched starts failing in production. What is missing from the lifecycle?
options: Continuous integration, because the merge was never validated.
A staging environment, because the change was never rehearsed.
Observability, because the team deployed but did not watch the running release.
Source control, because the change cannot be rolled back.
questions.explanation: A deployment that succeeds is not the same as a release that works. Observability is the discipline of understanding a running system from its outputs, and monitoring and feedback on a release are what close the DevOps loop. A deployment that lands and is never watched can fail for a week before anyone notices.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
Your integration can write a record to Salesforce, but that says nothing about who can see it.
The opposite is true: your integration can write a record to Salesforce, but that says nothing about who can see it.
The lesson claims this cannot be verified at all.
questions.explanation: Your integration can write a record to Salesforce, but that says nothing about who can see it.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Throughput is how many requests you complete per unit of time.
The lesson says the opposite: this should always be avoided.
Throughput is not how many requests you complete per unit of time.
The lesson claims this cannot be verified at all.
questions.explanation: Throughput is how many requests you complete per unit of time.

questions.question: A client wants a near-zero RPO on financial records but currently only takes daily backups. What does the lesson say is required beyond a more frequent backup?
options: Nothing; daily backups are sufficient to guarantee a near-zero RPO
A secondary data center added to the same org so it becomes active-active automatically
A replication mechanism such as asynchronous event streaming or Change Data Capture, because daily backups alone cap the RPO at a day
A legally binding service level agreement with the vendor that waives any data loss
questions.explanation: Near-zero RPO for financial transactions requires event-driven asynchronous replication, and minute-level RPO can use Change Data Capture. A daily backup cannot produce a sub-day recovery point.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Core Building Blocks: Objects, Fields, Relationships, Record Types, and Formula vs Roll-Up”, what is the central focus?
options: The architect's canvas: standard and custom objects, field types, lookup vs master-detail relationships, record types for process variation, and when to compute with a formula field vs a roll-up summary.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The architect's canvas: standard and custom objects, field types, lookup vs master-detail relationships, record types for process variation, and when to compute with a formula field vs a roll-up summary.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Lightning Performance: Caching, Static Resources, and What Slows Users Down”, an org created before Winter ’19 has never had Session Settings opened, and the team wants the cheapest real wins first. Which two changes cost nothing and can be made today?
options: Enable the CDN for the Lightning component framework after IT allowlists static.lightning.force.com, and confirm secure and persistent browser caching is enabled.
Move the chart library into a static resource, and cap the related list to the columns on screen.
Replace the wired Apex calls with Lightning Data Service adapters, and delete the components nobody uses.
Republish the site, and convert every component on the layout to lazy instantiation.
questions.explanation: Both are session settings, both are disabled by default only in older orgs, and together they address framework delivery and repeat-visit reloads before any code changes.

questions.question: Meridian's integration hub aggregates Salesforce, an ERP, a data warehouse, and a billing system. The ERP that feeds the hub authenticates with a shared human password that has not been rotated in years. Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance for the security model?
options: The model is only as strong as the least protected system in the chain, so the ERP's weak credential is a hole in the model even though Salesforce itself is well protected, and the model must be applied consistently to every system.
The ERP is outside Salesforce, so its authentication is the ERP vendor's responsibility and does not affect the enterprise security model.
Because Salesforce is the hub, securing Salesforce alone is sufficient to protect the data that flows through the hub.
A shared password is acceptable for system-to-system access as long as the data moves over an encrypted channel.
questions.explanation: The lesson states the weakest-link problem directly: a hub that aggregates five systems is only as safe as its weakest credential, and the model has to be applied consistently, not just to the systems you like. It also says system-to-system access must authenticate with a service credential, OAuth flow, or named credential, never a shared human password.

questions.question: Per the lesson “What a Salesforce System Architect Actually Does: Role, Cert Track, CTA Endgame”, what is the central focus?
options: The Salesforce architect arc in one lesson: what System vs Application vs Technical Architects actually do, the certification ladder, and the CTA endgame.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The Salesforce architect arc in one lesson: what System vs Application vs Technical Architects actually do, the certification ladder, and the CTA endgame.

questions.question: In the Aurora Manufacturing Group walkthrough, why does the order-placement integration use a queue that the ERP polls in batches rather than a synchronous call on every order save?
options: Because the lesson says synchronous calls are always an anti-pattern.
Because the ERP's SOAP API degrades badly under load, so the queue lets the ERP consume work at its own pace and protects the highest-volume operation.
Because Salesforce cannot send data to external systems in any other way.
Because the budget prohibits synchronous integration entirely.
questions.explanation: The ERP's SOAP API is reliable on small payloads but degrades under load. The highest-volume order-placement operation goes through a queue the ERP polls in batches, so the ERP consumes at its own pace, and every handler is idempotent so a retried delivery cannot create a duplicate fulfillment.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Federated Data: Salesforce Connect, External Objects, and When Not to Use Them”, what does query pushdown actually do?
options: It copies every matching row into Salesforce storage so later reads are local.
It translates the WHERE, ORDER BY, and LIMIT clauses into the source system's query and returns only the filtered result set.
It downloads the full external dataset into Salesforce and filters it locally in Apex.
It forces the source system into a synchronous write-back transaction for the matched rows.
questions.explanation: Query pushdown moves the query to the data: Salesforce translates the filters, ordering, and limit into the source's query and the source returns only the matching rows, so only the answer travels back to Salesforce.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Multi-Org Architecture: When to Split, and Org-to-Org Integration Patterns”, which situation is a legitimate structural reason to split, and which reason does it replace?
options: A regulatory or compliance walled-garden requirement, which replaces a slow request backlog as a reason to give a line of business its own org.
The lines of business wanting their own space, which is met with a center of excellence, delegated administration, and tiered data architecture instead of a split.
A regulatory or compliance walled-garden requirement that sharing alone cannot satisfy, because the requirement is structural isolation and reviewability, not record visibility.
A desire for a faster-paced release cycle, which a second org delivers with no added integration cost.
questions.explanation: The legitimate split is the one where the wall itself is the requirement, giving a compliance burden its own isolated org and reviewable audit trail, which a sharing model controls visibility but cannot deliver.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The opposite is true: the same-object relationship keeps the shape flat while expressing a tree.
The same-object relationship keeps the shape flat while expressing a tree.
The lesson states this is never a relevant consideration.
The lesson argues this applies only in unrelated settings.
questions.explanation: The same-object relationship keeps the shape flat while expressing a tree.

questions.question: A developer merges a change that breaks the integration build. Where does the team find out, and why does that matter?
options: In continuous integration, on the day of the merge, because CI validates every merge to the shared main line and catching the break there is cheap.
At release time, because integration is a separate phase that only runs before production.
In production, because that is the first environment where the change is actually exercised.
Never, because a broken integration build has no effect on the rest of the lifecycle.
questions.explanation: Continuous integration validates every merge to the shared main line, so a change that breaks the build is caught the day it is merged, not the week before release. Catching it in CI is cheap; catching it at release time is not.

questions.question: A hub's fan-out leg must call five external systems, but one of them is slow and risks consuming the whole latency budget. Per the lesson, what is the correct first design response for a read-side aggregation view?
options: Fire all five synchronous callouts from within the Apex transaction and accept that a slow system delays the whole page.
Move the fan-out off the synchronous request path or cache the composed result, so the hub does not pay the full fan-out cost on every visit.
Split the aggregation into animation the client can run while the callouts complete in parallel.
Increase the Apex callout limit per transaction above 100 to buy more headroom for the slow system.
questions.explanation: The lesson says the cumulative time for external callouts in a transaction cannot exceed 120 seconds, and a slow system eats time the others needed. When latency matters, the fix is caching the composed view or moving the fan-out off the request path, not paying the full cost on every visit.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: A canary that watches only error rate and latency is a software canary wearing an AI costume; hallucination rate, coherence, LLM-as-a-judge results, and business signals belong from the first stage.
Canary routing should be random per turn so the comparison sample stays balanced even mid-conversation.
Because outputs are nondeterministic, canary stages should be shortened so a regression is not masked by soak time.
A golden set of hand-written happy paths is the fastest route to a trustworthy offline score.
questions.explanation: A model can be technically flawless on the infrastructure dashboards and still produce worse reasoning or a tone shift, and nondeterminism means longer soak times rather than shorter ones.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Did the team reach for Apex when a Flow would do, or for a custom object when a standard one fits?
The opposite is true: did the team reach for Apex when a Flow would do, or for a custom object when a standard one fits?.
The lesson claims this cannot be verified at all.
The lesson argues this applies only in unrelated settings.
questions.explanation: Did the team reach for Apex when a Flow would do, or for a custom object when a standard one fits?

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Enterprise gets a Partial Copy but no Full sandbox by default, so a small Enterprise org that needs a staging replica must buy a Full license.
Enterprise gets a Partial Copy but no Full sandbox by default, so a small Enterprise org that needs a staging replica must not buy a Full license.
The lesson says the opposite: this should always be avoided.
The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
questions.explanation: Enterprise gets a Partial Copy but no Full sandbox by default, so a small Enterprise org that needs a staging replica must buy a Full license.

questions.question: Per the lesson “System Limits: Governor, API, and Storage Limits, and Planning Around Them”, what is the central focus?
options: Governors exist to keep a multitenant platform fair. Learn the limits, then bulkify, batch, and monitor so they never fire on your watch.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: Governors exist to keep a multitenant platform fair. Learn the limits, then bulkify, batch, and monitor so they never fire on your watch.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: If a user can see a child opportunity, case, contact, or order, they implicitly see the associated account, and the account hierarchy does not roll access up the way the role hierarchy does.
Implicit sharing applies to custom objects as well as standard parent-child pairings, and it can be disabled per object.
The account hierarchy rolls access up from a child account to its parent, exactly like the role hierarchy.
Implicit sharing is a configurable setting that an administrator turns on when parent access should follow child access.
questions.explanation: Implicit sharing is native and cannot be turned on or off, it only covers those standard parent-child pairings, and the account hierarchy is not a sharing relationship as the role hierarchy is.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Because the attention budget is finite and recall degrades as context grows, an eviction and summarization strategy is non-negotiable, and tool output has to be designed for context efficiency.
Longer context always improves recall, so a model with a large window should be filled with as much history as possible.
Memory without grounding is safe as long as the store is durable.
One-shot extraction and classification tasks should be built stateful so they improve across requests.
questions.explanation: Context rot means longer context does not mean better recall, so something must always leave the window and the decision about what that is belongs to the architecture, not to the raw transcript.

questions.question: A monthly load of 400,000 records runs as one REST call per record against an allocation of 280,000 calls per day, and a developer says the sandbox test finished in 40 minutes so it is fine. What is the correct reading?
options: The test proves capacity is sufficient, because 40 minutes is well inside the nightly window.

The load alone exceeds the daily allocation at 400,000 calls, so callers fail and retries make it worse. It should move to Bulk API 2.0, whose batches draw from a separate allocation pool, and the sandbox result only proved data volume behavior, not production concurrency.
The load is acceptable because REST calls are not counted against the API allocation when they run outside business hours.
The load is acceptable if the developer raises the batch size in the REST request payload.
questions.explanation: The lesson states that the cost unit is the call, not the record, so 400,000 records as individual REST calls consumes 400,000 calls against a 280,000 daily allocation. It also states that a full copy sandbox proves data-volume behavior and not concurrency, so a comfortable sandbox timing is a floor rather than a prediction.

questions.question: A partner's integration is spiking and draining the org's shared API request allocation. You put a gateway in front of the org and set per-consumer rate limits. Why does rejecting the over-budget partner at the gateway protect the org's allocation, rather than solving nothing?
options: Because the gateway routes the rejected call to a lower-cost API that does not count against the allocation.
Because calls refused by the gateway never reach Salesforce, so they burn the gateway's budget instead of the org's shared allocation.
Because Salesforce lifts the total allocation cap once the gateway reports a throttled tenant.
Because the gateway's limits replace the platform's concurrent API request limit entirely.
questions.explanation: The lesson's governing rule is to put policy at the boundary: authentication and rate limiting push as far out as possible so a misbehaving consumer burns the gateway's budget, not the org's. The Salesforce API request allocation is shared, finite, and enforced on the aggregate of all calls, so a call refused before reaching Salesforce never consumes it.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Multiple triggers on one object are preferable because each one stays small and readable.
All of an object’s rules, DML, and validation should live in the trigger file so the logic is easy to find.
One thin trigger per object that routes to handler and service classes restores ordered execution and stops redundant queries from sharing the same governor budget.
A recursion guard becomes unnecessary once bulkification is done, because triggers batch at 200 records anyway.
questions.explanation: A single entry point per object keeps the firing order explicit, keeps one budget in view, and moves the logic into classes that a unit test can call directly.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Experienced page time is measured on the server, so network conditions and device power cannot explain two users seeing different load times.
Server-side selectivity and indexing are the first thing to investigate when a Lightning page feels slow to users.
A wired Apex method that is not cacheable still benefits from the client cache, so the annotation has no performance effect.
Two users in the same org on the same page can legitimately see different experienced page time, because network and device set a floor that no org configuration controls.
questions.explanation: Network, device, browser, and configuration set the floor, and only the last is yours, which is why the server-side work comes after confirming the org-level caches are switched on.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: The earlier lessons handed you the mechanisms: integration patterns, reliability, environments, data architecture.
The lesson says only technical staff should act on this.
The lesson states this is never a relevant consideration.
The opposite is true: the earlier lessons handed you the mechanisms: integration patterns, reliability, environments, data architecture.
questions.explanation: The earlier lessons handed you the mechanisms: integration patterns, reliability, environments, data architecture.
